items.signature: company 2,500 employees, Plant B 750; random 50 of Plant B, 18 ride bus -> non-riders 32/50 x 750 = 480, which is 19.2% of 2,500; traps 64 (sample %), 30 (Plant B share), 7.2 / 10.8 (riders)
items.stem: A company has 2,500 employees, and 750 of them work at its Plant B. A random sample of 50 employees was selected from the employees at Plant B, and 18 of them said they ride a bus to work. Based on the sample, the employees at Plant B who do NOT ride a bus to work are estimated to make up what percent of all 2,500 employees of the company?

common_wrong.feedback: 64% is the share of Plant B’s sample who do not ride. The question uses all 2,500 employees as the base.
10.8% describes the Plant B bus riders, the wrong group.

solution.key_idea: Scale the sample only to the group it came from (Plant B). Then change the base to the whole company for the final percent.
solution.steps:
What does the question ask? A percent of ALL 2,500 employees, for one group: Plant B non-riders.
The sample came only from Plant B, so it can estimate counts for Plant B’s 750 employees, not for the other plants.
Step 1: Plant B share who do not ride.
$\frac{50 - 18}{50} = \frac{32}{50} = 0.64$ (non-riders in the sample)
Step 2: Estimate the count at Plant B.
$0.64 \times 750 = 480$ (Plant B has 750 employees)
Step 3: Change the base to the company.
$\frac{480}{2{,}500} = 0.192 = 19.2\%$ (part of all 2,500 employees)
solution.be_careful: The 2,500 is not the population of the sample; it is only the base of the final percent.
solution.another_way: Plant B is $30\%$ of the company, and $64\%$ of Plant B do not ride, so $0.30 \times 0.64 = 0.192$.

items.signature: goal: cause + all city adults. Designs: random sample let choose; volunteers randomly assigned; random sample + random assignment (key); random samples of users and non-users compared
items.stem: A researcher wants to determine whether using a certain sleep app causes adults in a city to sleep longer, and wants the conclusion to apply to all adults in the city. Which of the following study designs best meets both goals?

choices.text: Select 400 adults at random from the city, then let each adult decide whether to use the app.
choices.feedback: Random selection covers the city, but adults who choose the app may differ, so cause is not shown.

choices.text: Recruit 400 adult volunteers in the city, then randomly assign 200 of them to use the app.
choices.feedback: Random assignment supports cause, but volunteers do not represent all adults in the city.

choices.text: Select 400 adults at random from the city, then randomly assign 200 of them to use the app.
Select 200 app users and 200 nonusers at random from the city’s adults and compare them.
choices.feedback: Both samples are random, but the adults chose whether to use the app, so this is still observational.

solution.key_idea: To get cause for a whole population, a study needs random selection from that population AND random assignment to treatments.
solution.steps:
What does the question ask? A design that gives cause AND reaches all city adults.
Cause needs random assignment (chance decides who uses the app)
All city adults needs random selection (chance decides who is in the study)
Two random samples of users and nonusers: assignment? No (people still chose the app)
Only “select at random, then randomly assign” has both.
solution.check: Each other design is missing exactly one of the two random steps ✓
solution.be_careful: Two random SAMPLES of users and nonusers sound random, but nobody was assigned.
solution.another_way: Make a 2-column checklist (random selection, random assignment) and tick each design; only one gets two ticks.

items.signature: Study 1 random 1,000 county adults, tea drinkers lower BP (obs); Study 2 80 volunteers randomized tea vs water, tea lowered BP -> association in county + cause for volunteers-like; traps cause for all county (merge), Study 1 cause, neither
items.stem: Two studies looked at green tea and blood pressure. In Study 1, 1,000 adults were selected at random from a county, and those who drink green tea daily had lower blood pressure, on average. In Study 2, 80 adult volunteers were randomly assigned to drink green tea or water daily for 8 weeks, and the tea group’s blood pressure fell significantly more. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.text: Together, the two studies show that tea likely lowers blood pressure for all adults in the county.
choices.feedback: Combining studies does not combine their strengths: no single study had both random selection from the county and random assignment.

choices.text: Study 1 alone shows that drinking tea likely lowers blood pressure for all adults in the county.
choices.feedback: Study 1 is observational; tea drinkers chose to drink tea.

choices.text: Neither study supports any cause conclusion, because the two studies used different groups of adults.
choices.feedback: Study 2 used random assignment, so it supports cause for adults like its volunteers.

choices.text: Tea is linked to lower blood pressure in the county, and it likely lowers it for adults like the volunteers.

solution.key_idea: Each study supports only what its own design allows; two partial designs do not add up to one complete design.
solution.steps:
What does the question ask? The conclusion the two studies, each on its own terms, support.
Study 1: random selection, no assignment (association, for the county)
Study 2: assignment, volunteers (cause, for adults like the volunteers)
Merge them? No (no single group of people had both random steps)
So: a link in the county, and a likely cause for adults like the volunteers.
solution.check: Each half of the chosen conclusion matches one study’s design ✓
solution.be_careful: The tempting answer glues the two studies into a design that was never carried out.
solution.another_way: Ask of any cause claim for “all adults in the county”: which one study had random selection from the county AND random assignment? None.

items.signature: school 1,200; random 80 students, randomly assigned 44 reminders / 36 none; 33 vs 18 submitted all -> (0.75 - 0.5) x 1,200 = 300; traps 450 (15/40 equal-group), 900
items.stem: A high school has 1,200 students. A random sample of 80 of the students was selected, and the students were randomly assigned to two groups: 44 received daily homework reminders by text, and 36 did not. Of the students who received reminders, 33 turned in every homework assignment that month, and of the others, 18 did. Based on the study, how many more of the school’s 1,200 students are estimated to turn in every assignment if all receive reminders than if none do?

common_wrong.feedback: This uses the count difference $33 - 18 = 15$ as if each group had 40 students. The groups have 44 and 36 students.
900 is the number expected to turn in every assignment WITH reminders, not how many more.

solution.key_idea: Random assignment makes the difference in rates an estimate of the effect; random selection lets that effect be scaled to the whole school.
solution.steps:
What does the question ask? (all reminded) $-$ (none reminded), for 1,200 students.
Two facts make this possible: random assignment (so the difference is caused by the reminders) and random selection from the school (so it can be scaled to all 1,200).
Step 1: Rate in each group.
reminders: $\frac{33}{44} = 0.75$ (33 of the 44)
no reminders: $\frac{18}{36} = 0.5$ (18 of the 36)
Step 2: Scale to the school.
$0.75 \times 1{,}200 = 900$ (expected with reminders)
$0.5 \times 1{,}200 = 600$ (expected without)
Step 3: Finish line.
$900 - 600 = 300$ (how many more)
solution.be_careful: Unequal groups: divide each count by its own group size before comparing.
solution.another_way: The reminders raise the rate by 25 out of every 100 students; the school has 12 hundreds, so $25 \times 12 = 300$.

skill.cb_skill: Evaluating statistical claims: Observational studies and experiments

items.signature: 60 volunteers randomly assigned keyboards, but new group tested at 9 a.m., old at 4 p.m. -> time of day confounds; traps not random sample (scope, not cause for these), too few, should let choose
items.stem: A researcher randomly assigned 60 office-worker volunteers to type on either a new keyboard or their usual keyboard. Everyone using the new keyboard was tested at 9:00 a.m., and everyone using the usual keyboard was tested at 4:00 p.m. The new-keyboard group typed faster. The researcher concluded that, for these volunteers, the new keyboard caused faster typing. Which of the following is the strongest criticism of this conclusion?

choices.text: Workers may type differently early and late in the day, so the time could explain the result.
The volunteers were not selected at random from all office workers in the country.
choices.feedback: True, but the conclusion was only about these volunteers, so this does not weaken it.

choices.text: The volunteers should have been allowed to choose which keyboard they used.
choices.feedback: Letting them choose would make the groups LESS comparable.

choices.text: Sixty volunteers is too few people for random assignment to have any effect.
choices.feedback: Sixty is enough for random assignment to balance the groups on average; the problem is the testing times.

solution.key_idea: Random assignment only supports cause if the groups are then treated the same in every other way.
solution.steps:
What does the question ask? The criticism that actually weakens “the keyboard caused it, for these volunteers”.
Assignment was random (good start)
But each group was tested at a different time (a second difference between the groups)
Morning vs late afternoon (tiredness can change typing speed)
So the time of day, not the keyboard, could explain the result.
The criticism about random selection is true but misses: the conclusion was only about these volunteers.
solution.check: Testing both groups at mixed times would remove the criticism ✓
solution.be_careful: A criticism must hit the claim that was made. The claim was limited to the volunteers, so “not a random sample” misses.
solution.another_way: List every way the two groups differ: keyboard AND test time. Two differences means the effect cannot be pinned on one.

items.signature: random 150 farms in region, drip farms higher yield -> only "among region farms, drip farms tend to have higher yields"; traps switch -> rise (cause), stop -> fall (counterfactual cause), all farms in country
items.stem: An agency selected 150 farms at random from all farms in a region and found that farms using drip irrigation had higher crop yields per acre, on average, than farms not using it. Which of the following statements is best supported by this information?

choices.text: A farm in the region that switches to drip irrigation will likely see its yield per acre rise.
choices.feedback: Predicting what happens when a farm CHANGES is a cause claim; the farms chose their own irrigation.

choices.text: Among farms in the region, those using drip irrigation tend to have higher yields per acre.
Farms in the region now using drip irrigation would likely have lower yields if they stopped.
choices.feedback: This is also a cause claim, about what would happen without drip irrigation.

choices.text: Among all farms in the country, those using drip irrigation tend to have higher yields per acre.
choices.feedback: Only farms in this region could be selected.

solution.key_idea: Any statement about what would happen if something CHANGED is a cause claim, even without the word “cause”.
solution.steps:
What does the question ask? The one statement this observational study supports.
Random selection: farms in the region (scope = the region)
Random assignment: none (no cause claims)
“switches → rise” and “stopped → lower” (both predict effects of a change: cause)
So only the “tend to have” statement about farms in the region is supported.
The country-wide statement has the right strength (association) but the wrong scope.
solution.check: The chosen statement describes a pattern among existing farms and stays in the region ✓
solution.be_careful: Cause claims can hide in “if … then … will” sentences.
solution.another_way: Drip farms may be newer or richer; those differences, not the irrigation, could explain the yields, which is why change-predictions are unsupported.

skill.cb_skill: Evaluating statistical claims: Observational studies and experiments

items.signature: 500 selected, 320 responded, 208 support -> greatest possible percent of the 500: (208 + 180)/500 = 77.6; traps 65 (of responders), 41.6 (least)
items.stem: A town selected 500 residents at random and asked whether they support a new park. Of the 500 selected residents, 320 responded, and 208 of those who responded said they support the park. If every selected resident has an opinion, what is the greatest possible percent of the 500 selected residents who support the park?

common_wrong.feedback: 65% is $\frac{208}{320}$, the percent of RESPONDERS. It assumes the 180 nonresponders split the same way.
41.6% is the LEAST possible percent, when none of the nonresponders support the park.

solution.key_idea: Nonresponders’ opinions are unknown, so the true percent of those selected can be anywhere from “none of them agree” to “all of them agree”.
solution.steps:
What does the question ask? The GREATEST possible percent of all 500 selected residents.
We know the answers of only 320 people. The rest could support or oppose, so to make the percent as large as possible, assume every nonresponder supports the park.
nonresponders: $500 - 320 = 180$ (their opinions are unknown)
greatest: all 180 support (the most supporters possible)
supporters $= 208 + 180 = 388$ (known plus all unknown)
$\frac{388}{500} = 0.776 = 77.6\%$ (percent of the 500)
solution.check: Least possible: $\frac{208}{500} = 41.6\%$; the true value lies between 41.6% and 77.6%, and 65% is inside ✓
solution.be_careful: 65% quietly assumes the nonresponders think like the responders.
solution.another_way: Count the residents who do NOT support for sure: $320 - 208 = 112$. At most $500 - 112 = 388$ can support.

skill.cb_skill: Evaluating statistical claims: Observational studies and experiments

items.signature: 2x2 randomized: no fert/normal 30.4, no/extra 33.1, fert/normal 34.0, fert/extra 38.9 -> fertilizer effect 3.6 (normal) and 5.8 (extra), difference 2.2; traps 3.6, 5.8, 8.5 (diagonal)
items.stem:
A scientist randomly assigned 120 pepper plants to four groups of 30. Each group received a different combination of fertilizer (none or some) and watering (normal or extra). The table shows the mean height of each group after 6 weeks.
Mean height (cm)Normal wateringExtra watering
No fertilizer30.433.1
Fertilizer34.038.9
Based on the experiment, the fertilizer’s estimated effect on mean height is how many centimeters greater for plants that receive extra watering than for plants that receive normal watering?

common_wrong.feedback: 5.8 is the fertilizer’s effect with extra watering only; the question compares it with the effect under normal watering.
8.5 compares fertilizer with extra watering to no fertilizer with normal watering: two things changed at once.

solution.key_idea: A treatment’s effect is a difference between two groups that differ ONLY in that treatment. Find the fertilizer effect within each watering level, then compare the two effects.
solution.steps:
What does the question ask? How much LARGER the fertilizer effect is with extra watering than with normal watering.
The plants were randomly assigned, so the groups differ only in their treatments. Each fertilizer effect must compare two groups with the SAME watering.
Step 1: Fertilizer effect with normal watering.
$34.0 - 30.4 = 3.6$ (Normal watering column)
Step 2: Fertilizer effect with extra watering.
$38.9 - 33.1 = 5.8$ (Extra watering column)
Step 3: Compare the two effects.
$5.8 - 3.6 = 2.2$ (how many centimeters greater)
solution.check: Same result by rows: watering effect with fertilizer $38.9 - 34.0 = 4.9$, without $33.1 - 30.4 = 2.7$, and $4.9 - 2.7 = 2.2$ ✓
solution.be_careful: Do not stop at 5.8, and never subtract across a diagonal: that changes fertilizer AND watering.
solution.another_way: Both columns change only the fertilizer, so each gives a fair effect; the answer is the gap between those two fair effects.

items.signature: random 300 of adults aged 18-30 in County R, randomly assigned meditation app; app group lower stress -> NOT supported: all ages in County R; supported: 18-30 cause, participants means, difference unlikely from chance alone
items.stem: Researchers selected 300 adults at random from all adults aged 18 to 30 in County R and randomly assigned half of them to use a meditation app daily. After 8 weeks, the app group had a significantly lower mean stress score than the other group. Which of the following is NOT supported by the study?

choices.text: For adults aged 18 to 30 in County R, the app likely lowers mean stress scores.
choices.feedback: This IS supported: random selection from that age group plus random assignment.

choices.text: For the 300 participants, the app group’s mean stress score was lower.
choices.feedback: This IS supported: it simply restates the result.

choices.text: For adults of all ages in County R, the app likely lowers mean stress scores.
The groups’ difference is unlikely to be due only to chance in the assignment.
choices.feedback: This IS supported: “significantly lower” means the difference is too large to be explained by chance alone.

solution.key_idea: Even a study with both random steps reaches only the population it sampled, including its age limits.
solution.steps:
What does the question ask? The ONE statement that goes too far.
Random selection: adults aged 18 to 30 in County R (scope)
Random assignment: yes (cause is allowed)
“adults of all ages in County R” (older adults could not be selected)
So the all-ages statement is not supported.
Check the others: the 18-to-30 statement matches the design, the participant statement restates the result, and “significantly” means chance alone is an unlikely explanation.
solution.check: The other three statements stay within the age limit or within the 300 participants ✓
solution.be_careful: In NOT questions, the right answer is a statement that sounds fine but breaks one limit.
solution.another_way: Strong designs make students relax; reread the population line word by word: “aged 18 to 30”.
